analysis.one_liner: Ties federal loan backing for manufactured home parks to basic tenant rights like lease renewals, rent-increase notice, and home-sale protections.
analysis.headline: The bill would tie federal loan backing for manufactured home community buyers to basic tenant rights, but it has sat in the Senate Banking Committee since its introduction with no action taken.
analysis.plain_summary: About 20 million Americans live in manufactured homes, where they usually own the house but rent the land underneath it, leaving them exposed to sudden rent hikes or closure of the community. This bill would say that if a community owner wants federally backed loans — loans insured by HUD or bought by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — the owner must give residents a set of minimum rights: renewable one-year leases, at least 60 days' notice before rent increases or a sale or closure, a grace period on late rent, and the right to sell their home in place instead of moving it. Owners who break the rules could be cut off from federal financing and owe tenants money. The bill also would create a commission to propose stronger protections over time.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of manufactured home communities — disproportionately lower-income and older Americans — gain stable one-year leases, advance notice and justification of rent increases, a grace period on rent, the ability to sell their home without moving it, notice before a community is sold or closed, and defined payments from owners who violate the rules. Because the protections attach to federal financing that large corporate owners of parks use heavily, they would reach the big investors who dominate the market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Manufactured home residents who rent their lots

how_it_helps.text: Federally backed loans would be available only to community owners who give residents one-year renewable leases unless there is good cause for non-renewal.

Owners would have to give written notice of rent increases at least 60 days ahead, with extra notice tacked on for larger increases and a written justification of the increase tied to operating costs.

Residents would gain a 5-day grace period on rent, a right to cure missed payments within 15 days, the right to sell their home in place rather than move it, the right to post For Sale signs, and the right to pass their lease to a home buyer.

Residents would get 60 days' notice before a sale or closure of the community, including the price and terms, and the owner would have to negotiate in good faith for 60 days if residents want to buy the community themselves.

Owners who willfully violate the protections could be barred from future federally backed financing for at least two years and would owe tenants defined payments, such as six months' rent for improper eviction or 25 percent over the increased rent for a notice violation.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of manufactured home communities, especially large corporate investors, would bear the cost: lease restrictions, rent-increase notice and justification requirements, limits on terminating tenants, penalties including repayment to tenants with interest plus 25 percent, and potential two-year bans from federal financing for willful violations. Some owners might respond by seeking non-federal financing to escape the conditions.

drawbacks.text: The protections only apply to loans backed by HUD, Fannie Mae, or Freddie Mac; owners who take out conventional financing with no federal backstop would not have to offer these tenant rights, so many communities could remain outside the bill's reach.

The bill says no additional funds are authorized, leaving enforcement to existing HUD and FHFA staff and budgets, which could make policing violations and paying the specified tenant damages slower or thinner than the paper penalties suggest.

Owners could face real costs: lease restrictions on rent increases and terminations, buyback obligations if they improperly block a home sale, and multi-penalty damages, which critics would argue could discourage investment in maintaining or purchasing communities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for residents are concrete and the costs fall on owners of manufactured home communities, who would face lease restrictions, notice requirements, and penalties when using federal financing; some owners might instead avoid federally backed loans or slow new community purchases, which could modestly reduce available financing for communities. On balance the trade is favorable to the roughly 20 million people who live in manufactured homes and face some of the least regulated tenancy terms in housing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and referred to the Banking Committee, where it has sat with no further action; nothing indicates the committee plans to take it up.

narrative.text: Senator Shaheen introduced the bill on March 27, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
No further action has been taken since that referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action is listed in the bill's action history.

Under the bill, HUD could not insure and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac could not purchase loans for manufactured home communities unless the owner certified tenant protections including one-year renewable leases, 60-day notice of rent increases, a five-day rent grace period, and the right to sell a home in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of manufactured home communities, including large corporate and private-equity buyers, are better off because no restrictions have been attached to the federally backed financing they rely on; residents gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate park owners relying on federal financing

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its tenant-protection conditions on federal financing.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal and John Fetterman

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral with no hearing, markup, or vote on record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only supporters on record are three Democratic senators; no Republican has signed on and no one has opposed it on the record — the bill has simply not moved.

industries.industry: Manufactured home community owners and investors (including large corporate owners)
industries.note: Owners using federally backed loans would have to accept lease restrictions, rent-increase notice rules, sale and closure notice duties, and tenant-damage penalties. Because large investors rely heavily on Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and HUD financing, this is where the bill would bind them most.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and the government-sponsored enterprises (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac)
industries.note: Lenders would face new certification, documentation, and compliance requirements on manufactured community loans, though the bill would also ban pricing discounts unless they reward protections stricter than the bill's minimums, standardizing a market they already serve.

industries.industry: Residents of manufactured home communities (roughly 20 million people, mostly lower-income)
industries.note: Residents would gain lease stability, notice of rent hikes and closures, and the ability to sell their homes in place. They own the home but not the land, which is exactly what makes them vulnerable to rent increases and eviction.

analysis.trajectory: The bill was referred to Senate Banking in March 2025 and has seen no action since; first-term Senate housing bills without bipartisan sponsorship or a committee markup rarely advance, so it is likely to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless a hearing or cosponsor surge changes the picture.
